titleStmt.title: Refining Task Specifications Using Model Checking

analytic.title: Refining Task Specifications Using Model Checking

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The problem of schedulability analysis, i.e., determining whether a given task set meets its deadline constraints, has been extensively studied in the real-time systems literature. However, if a task set is not schedulable, then the schedulability analysis results using known techniques (such as utilization-based tests) offer little insight into which task parameters could be changed or refined, in order to make the task set schedulable.

To address this problem, we encode the schedulability analysis problem as an equivalent model checking problem. By analyzing the counterexamples reported by the model checker, we discover subsets of values of task parameters that lead to timing violations. We propose a procedure that iteratively refines the task specification by rejecting these subsets, thereby converging towards schedulability. We believe that this approach would be useful for timing debugging of real-time systems, which has received relatively less attention in the literature, especially given its practical relevance.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Schedulability analysis checks whether a task set meets its deadline constraints under all possible scenarios. Often, when a task set is not schedulable, task parameters like task offsets, periods, and execution times (e.g., by recompiling the tasks with different optimization flags) might be revised to make the task set schedulable. However, most of the known techniques (such as utilization-based tests) offer little insight into which task parameters could be adjusted (refined), to make the task set schedulable. Since a task set might have multiple tasks, with each task having multiple parameters, there might be too many refinement choices for either exhaustive or ad hoc exploration, which we call timing debugging. There has been relatively less work on addressing this issue. In this paper, we investigate the role of model checking to address a subproblem in timing debugging, namely automatically refining task offsets to yield schedulable task sets.

We encode the task set along with the scheduling policy as a model, and the deadline constraint serves as a property. If the model violates the property, then the task set is not schedulable, and the counterexample returned by the model checker can provide valuable insights into which task parameters could be refined to make the task set schedulable. Given the large number of choices for refinement, this allows a systematic approach to timing debugging with the following benefits :-

• Automatic discovery and pruning of ranges of parameter values that contribute to unschedulability of the task set. • Counterexamples can be used to iteratively modify the task set parameters to make the task set schedulable. The main challenges in employing a model checker for schedulability analysis are (a) accurately and efficiently modelling (encoding) the scheduling policy, task sets and the timing property of interest, (b) when the model checker produces a counterexample demonstrating a violation of the timing property, how to use the counterexample to refine the task parameters, and (c) scalability to reasonably sized task sets.

Towards the challenge (a) above, we present an encoding of timing behaviours of tasks under various scheduling policies in a uniprocessor setting, which can be extended to the multiprocessor setting. Our encoding models the tasks, scheduling policy and architecture as a set of constraints in the language of a model checker such that schedulability property naturally translates into state reachability property in the model.

Towards challenge (b) above, suppose model checking the encoding reveals that a task instance misses its deadline. We then use the reported counterexample to search through the space of task parameters such as offset, to synthesize new values that meet the requirements. In particular, we present a sound iterative refinement algorithm based on Z3 [1], an optimizing SMT solver, that computes and prunes ranges of parameters that lead to the deadline violation. In our experimentation on task sets containing up to 10 tasks, our approach successfully analyzed all the task sets in under 2 minutes in a uniprocessor setting, thus addressing challenge (c) above. Together, the solutions to the above challenges form the main contribution of this paper.

As our work is mostly exploratory in nature, we choose earliest-deadline-first as a popular representative for dynamic priority scheduling, and rate-monotonic for static priority scheduling schemes. We focus on non-preemptive (NP) scheduling, as NP is the choice in safety-critical domains. Our approach can be extended to more complex task models and scheduling policies where timing debugging is even more challenging, for which even standard schedulability analysis techniques would not work.

div.head: A. Motivating example
div.p: Consider a task set shown in Table I-A, slightly adapted from [2]. Under both earliest-deadline-first and rate-monotonic scheduling policies, task 1 misses its deadline: the second instance, released at time 10 units with deadline 20, is scheduled only after task 3 finishes execution, which in the best case, is 22. The execution of task 3 is causing a problem.

To make this task set schedulable, suppose we allow the offset parameter to be varied. Note that for all values of offsets for task 3 in the range [0,10], the deadline miss is unavoidable. For each of these offsets, there is a schedule, with some combination of jitter and execution time values of the tasks, leading to the deadline miss. The task set, however, is schedulable if we change the offset of task 3 to 11.

The key challenges in restructuring task sets to meet schedulability are (i) an efficient schedulability analysis of task specifications admitting non-determinism, and (ii) for task parameters, systematically compute and prune bad instantiations.

div.head: B. Related work
div.p: Model checking with counterexample-guided abstraction refinement was introduced by Graf et al. [3] and Clarke et al. [4]. Model checking for schedulability analysis has been explored by several researchers. Fersman et al. [5] modelled fixedpriority uniprocessor scheduling as a reachability analysis on timed automata, using two extra clocks. This helped scale the model checking engine. Guan et al. [6] used the UPPAL model checker [7] to propose an exact method for static-priority multiprocessor schedulability analysis. Their technique transforms the schedulability problem into reachability analysis problem of timed automata. It supports preemption but discretizes the timed model. An improvement to this technique was proposed by Yu et al. [8] by using the Nu-SMV model checker [9]. The technique enabled schedulability and response time analysis of global multiprocessor scheduling, under fixed-priority and earliest-deadline-first scheduling policy. In [10], Gu et al. expanded the approach further to model task specifications with fixed offsets. The technique admitted non-determinism in task specification such as (bounded) jitter in the release time and execution time interval. The technique took advantage of the stopwatch feature introduced in UPPAL 4.1, to model preemption in tasks. An approach to check schedulability of task sets using SMT solvers is presented by Pedro et al. [11]. None of these approaches, however, refine task specifications to meet timing properties.

Nasri et al. [2], [12] discuss idle-time insertion policy for non-preemptive EDF and RM scheduling policies, which aims to improve schedulability of task sets in an online setting. The technique proposes to augment the scheduler with heuristics and rules to relax work conservation, enabling more task sets to be scheduled. Bini et al. [13], Seto et al. [14] present an analytical approach to sensitivity analysis, varying task computation time and period to improve schedulability. However, there are several restrictions on the class of task sets that can be scheduled in this way, and non-determinism in task specification is not supported.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL FOR UNIPROCESSOR SCHEDULING
div.p: Let T be a finite set of periodic tasks, to be scheduled on a processor. τ i ∈ T is specified as tid, period, BCET, WCET, oset, jitter, deadline, wcrt , where tid = i is a unique task id, period is the task period, [BCET,WCET] is the execution time interval of the task corresponding to best-and worst-case, oset (optional) is the task offset, jitter (optional) is the maximum jitter permitted for each instance of the task, deadline is the task deadline, and wcrt (optional) denotes the maximum response time permitted for the task i.e., the task must complete execution within wcrt time after its release.

Tasks spawn jobs. The jth job spawned by task τ i is released at time r i,j = j × period i + oset i . With jitter, the job is released at a non-deterministic (discrete) time point in the interval [r i,jjitter i , r i,j + jitter i ]. When the deadline is implicit, it can be computed as d i,j = (j +1)×period i +oset i . We denote with s i,j and e i,j , the start and end time of the job.

We assume that (i) the jobs spawned by tasks may terminate at any point in the discrete time interval [BCET,WCET] (ii) new jobs are scheduled at discrete time points under the scheduling policy on the processor.

A run of the system of tasks can be viewed as a sequence of jobs (s i,0 , e i,0 ), ... , that respects the scheduling policy. Given the non-determinism in task specification, many sequences are possible. We aim to encode all valid sequences of the system by guessing the start and end times of the jobs. Constraints arising from the task specification, scheduling policy and platform restrict the guesses such that the solutions to the set of constraints exactly represent valid sequences. Schedulability analysis can be carried out by introducing reachability assertions that check if any job has missed its deadline.

div.head: A. The timestore data structure
div.p: Let {tid, rtime, stime, etime, deadline} be a collection of arrays that guess the task id, release time, start time, end time, and deadline, respectively, for each job. We call this collection a task set timestore. Let loc represent an arbitrary location in the timestore. Our aim is to encode all valid sequences of the system, by appropriately constraining the guesses within the timestore. To check schedulability of the task set, it is sufficient to enumerate and check times of jobs spawned up to the hyper period of the task set, or the least common multiple of the periods of the tasks. If the etime for any job is larger than its deadline, for all possible guesses, the task set can be rejected as non-schedulable. However, to keep the analysis tractable, we may need to bound the number of jobs spawned, or the time horizon H of the system.

div.head: B. Initialization constraints
div.p: The size of the timestore is the maximum number of jobs spawned within a user-specified analysis time H. Usually, H will be the hyper period of the task periods so that all possible behaviours are checked. We begin with adding constraints that ensure that the timestore produces a sequence of jobs.

C. task spec constraints jobs store their guesses in unique locations in the timestore. each job must satisfy constraints arising from the task specification, namely the release time and execution time.
div.formula: ∀i, j, ∃loc : stime[loc] >= rtime[loc] ∧ ri,j -jitteri <= rtime[loc] <= ri,j + jitteri ∧ BCETi <= etime[loc] -stime[loc] <= WCETi (2)

div.head: D. Work conservation constraints
div.p: Work conserving schemes restrict the processor from being idle whenever there is a task that is ready to run. Due to the non-deterministic choice of start times of jobs in the timestore, jobs can "float" around. We need to add constraints that guarantee work conservation: jobs should get scheduled as soon as the processor is available. We need to constrain the job waiting time as follows.
Necessary condition. We first constrain a job's start time to coincide with the previous job's end time in the timestore, if this job has a waiting time.

This constraint is necessary but not sufficient, as it is possible to construct a job sequence that satisfies the constraint but is invalid: a job released earlier can have its start time coincide with the end time of a job released later, leaving the processor idle, thereby violating work conservation.

Sufficiency condition. Next, we need to examine all intervals in the timestore sequence where the processor is idle. For every idle interval found in the sequence, there should not exist a job that was released earlier than this interval but was scheduled after the gap.
div.formula: ∀loc : etime[loc -1] < stime[loc] ⇒ loc : rtime[loc ] < etime[loc -1] ∧ stime[loc ] > stime[loc]
div.p: We simplify the above double quantification constraint by constructing a global cut off on release time invariant on the timestore as follows. We add a new array cutoff to the timestore, that is constrained to be non-decreasing a-priori. Whenever there is an interval between any pair of successive jobs in the sequence, we advance the threshold for all future jobs (wrt the succeeding job in this pair) i.e., all future jobs are constrained to be released not earlier than the release time of this job.
div.formula: ∀loc, cutoff[loc -1] <= cutoff[loc] ∧ cutoff[loc] <= rtime[loc] ∧ etime[loc -1] < stime[loc] ⇒ cutoff[loc] = rtime[loc] (4)

div.head: E. Scheduling policy constraints 1) Earliest Deadline First:
div.p: The EDF scheduling policy mandates that at any scheduling point, the job chosen to execute must have the earliest deadline amongst all jobs that are ready-to-run at this point in time. Thus, in a sequence of jobs scheduled under EDF, jobs appear sorted on their deadlines, modulo their release times.

Consider a pair of jobs at locations loc, loc with loc < loc , in the timestore sequence. Since the job at location loc was scheduled earlier than the other, it must be that either the former had an earlier deadline, or the latter was released after the former was scheduled. This gives us the implication rtime[loc ] <= stime[loc] ⇒ deadline[loc] < deadline [loc ]. This constraint has to be checked for all jobs at locations following loc. Thus, for each loc, ∀loc s.t. loc < loc :

2) Rate Monotonic: The Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling policy assigns priorities to tasks, statically ordered by their periods. Thus, at any scheduling instant, the task having highest priority i.e., least period, is selected for execution amongst the ready-to-run tasks.

To encode RM scheduling policy, we assume the timestore is augmented with a new array prio that stores the (statically known) priority of each task. Similar to the EDF constraint explained above, we obtain the implication rtime[loc ] <= stime[loc] ⇒ prio[loc] > prio [loc ] for loc < loc i.e., for every pair of ready-to-run jobs at any scheduling instant, the one with higher priority is scheduled first. Again, this constraint needs to be checked across the timestore. Thus, f or each loc, ∀loc s.t. loc < loc :

The scheduling policy thus generates an order of n 2 constraints for n jobs in the system. The system of constraints from Eqn. 1-6 can be put together to obtain a correct-by-construction encoding of all runs of the task system under uniprocessor scheduling. Timing properties can be inserted as assertions, to be checked by a model checker such as CBMC [15].

div.head: F. Proof of correctness of the encoding
div.p: Lemma II.1. Every run of the specified tasks, under a given scheduling policy, exists as a solution to the set of constraints 1-6. Conversely, every solution to the constraints maps to a run of the tasks.

Proof. We give proof by contradiction. Suppose there exists a run of the tasks, bounded by the analysis time H, but violates one or more constraints listed above. Clearly, it cannot violate the initialization constraint of Eqn. 1, task specification constraint of Eqn. 2 or scheduling policy constraints Eqns. 5, 6, as otherwise the run would be trivially invalid.

The run cannot violate the necessary condition presented in Eqn. 3, as that would imply that some job had a nonzero waiting time but did not start execution as soon as the job scheduled prior to this finished, thereby violating work conservation.

Suppose the run did violate the sufficiency condition presented in Eqn. 4. This means for this run, we cannot construct the cut off invariant i.e., there is no non-decreasing array cutoff that, for every idle period of the processor, forces the jobs scheduled after this idle period to be also released after the idle period. In other words, this run has a job scheduled such that there is an idle period between its release and start of execution, violating work conservation. Thus this run is invalid. The converse can be similarly established.

Remark. When H corresponds to the hyper period of the tasks, then all behaviours are analyzed within time H. This takes care of runs extending beyond H. If the analysis up to H is not tractable due to model checking scalability limitations, then the results are limited to discovering timing violations within the time bound H, which is akin to bounded model checking of software [15].

div.head: III. REFINING TASK SPECIFICATIONS
div.p: Consider a task set implementing some control algorithms. During implementation phase, apart from the control tasks, additional tasks may get clubbed for execution with the control tasks such as logging, diagnostic, or domain-specific operations. This limits the time available for control computation. Current schedulability tests are generally pessimistic and may deem the task set to be non-schedulable in tight situations. We may thus have a situation where the task set might meet the control system performance, for given choice of task parameters such as offset, jitter, period and execution time, but deemed unschedulable. Unfortunately, neither the schedulability test, nor the control-theoretic analysis helps the system designer to improve the situation.

We propose to restructure the task set by automatically tuning the parameters within some acceptable range. In the control theory domain, it is well known that certain task parameters are more sensitive to control performance than others e.g., offset is less sensitive compared to say, period. Change to offset values, within some bound, does not significantly affect control performance of the embedded application, but can qualify the restructured task set to be schedulable. We use this domain knowledge, combined with the ability of model checkers to yield counterexamples pin-pointing timing problems in task sets, to give an iterative search procedure that refines task specifications. The refinement can be driven towards improving schedulability or meeting other timing requirements.

div.head: A. Modifying offset values
div.p: As an example of task specification refinement, we present a search procedure built on the encoding presented in Section II, that iteratively modifies task offsets to yield schedulability. We believe that the approach can be extended for tuning other task parameters like worst-case execution time, jitter and even task periods. We assume EDF scheduling policy, though the approach is fully applicable to other policies like RM. Our approach can be extended to the multiprocessor setting.

The approach adjusts offsets (within a given bound), leaving the period, execution time and jitter to their designer-specified values. The offset space is n-dimensional, where n is the number of tasks. The problem then, is to discover a point in this space that will lead to successful schedulability of the given task set. The approach uses counterexamples showing deadline misses, to identify and remove partitions from the offset space of the tasks, such that every point in the rejected partition preserves the witnessed deadline miss.

Given a task set that the model checker finds to be nonschedulable, consider the first job j i,k in the timestore sequence that missed its deadline i.e., e i,k > deadline i,k . The job missed its deadline due to contiguous scheduling of higher priority jobs during its waiting time i.e., in the interval [r i,k , s i,k ]. If we consider increasing the offset incrementally for this task, we can find an interval of offsets such that this job will continue to miss its deadline, in the same trace, assuming rest is unchanged. This interval is simply
div.formula: [oset i , oset i + e i,k -deadline i,k -1],
div.p: where oset i was the initial choice of offset for this task. Intuitively, the interval of offsets corresponds to the amount of time by which j i,k overshot its deadline i.e., the job will continue to miss its deadline until and unless a modified offset compensates for the required execution budget, other things remaining same. The offset can be similarly decremented, ensuring deadline miss, up to a time where j i,k gains higher priority over the preceding job. Now consider the set of jobs that were scheduled during the waiting time of j i,k . If we similarly stretch the offsets of these jobs, subject to certain constraints, we can again observe that j i,k will continue to miss its deadline. To illustrate this, consider job j i ,k scheduled before j i,k . Since j i ,k has a priority higher than j i,k , the constraint on increasing the offset is that the priority of j i ,k continues to remain higher than that of j i,k . We can thus obtain an interval
div.formula: [oset i ,k , oset i ,k + Δ], subject to (i) r i ,k <= s i,k , and (ii) deadline i ,k < deadline i,k .
div.p: We can similarly try to decrease the offsets for the set of jobs that were scheduled contiguously after j i,k , such that their priorities turn higher than that of j i,k , causing these jobs to be scheduled earlier than j i,k , and thus continuing the deadline miss for j i,k . We formalize and use this observation of task offset monotonocity, in the next subsection.

div.head: B. Discovering deadline miss-preserving intervals on offsets
div.p: Our proposed key search strategy is to discover these deadline miss-preserving intervals on task offsets, from each counterexample obtained. To maximize the interval size, we need to generalize the above heuristics by considering the cumulative effect of modifying offsets and the non-determinism inducing parameters such as jitter and execution time.

Further, multiple task runs are possible for each choice of offsets, corresponding to the combinatorial choices of these parameters. Some of these runs may preserve the deadline miss, some may cause another job to miss its deadline, and some others may correspond to different sequences altogether, both "good" and "bad". Even when the sequences are identical, they may differ in release, start or end times of jobs.

Any optimization procedure that tries to maximize (or minimize) the offsets, needs to be sound in the following sense: every point within the interval must be a "bad" offset, leading to a deadline miss. Thus the optimization needs to be combined with a decision procedure such that the optimization samples only from the space of "bad" traces, and in addition, must quantify over the interval it computes.

The former condition can be implemented by enumerating the points and invoking a model checker on each candidate. This loop can be constructed explicitly or using the maximization feature of an optimizing SMT solver like Z3 (which implements the loop implicitly.) We propose to implement the latter condition using Z3 as follows: we ask Z3 to maximize the interval subject to the obtained counterexample sequence embedded in the timestore. Intuitively, having discovered one "bad" sequence, we search in its neighborhood to obtain a sound interval. Thus, we pose the maximization problem:
div.formula: Maxo i SchedT ∧ φi,k ∧ ce timestore (7)
div.p: where o i is the offset of the task chosen for maximization, Sched T is the encoding of the task set T for checking schedulability, φ i,k is the constraint stating "job j i,k misses its deadline", ce is the earlier discovered (bad) sequence where j i,k was the first job missing its deadline, and denotes that the timestore is constrained to contain the sequence ce.

Lemma III.1 (Soundness). Eqn. 7 guarantees that for each (discrete) point within the computed interval, at least one job misses its deadline i.e., each point in the maximized interval is a "bad" offset.

Proof. To see how this satisfies the soundness condition, consider a point o j in the maximized interval [o i , o max ] where o i was the initial offset. Since o max preserves the sequence (by construction of Eqn. 7) originally yielded by o i , o max indicates the maximum disturbance possible to the offset o i without changing the sequence itself and the same (at least one) deadline miss. Since o j < o max , the disturbance posed by o j cannot reject this sequence i.e., all disturbances to the start, end, release or deadline times of the jobs within the timestore still preserve the sequence ce. Further, since both o i and o max violate the deadline of j i,k , there is at least one run corresponding to offset o j with at least j i,k missing its deadline. Many other sequences and behaviours might be possible with offset o j , which are not of concern to us.

Remark. If we do not include the constraint ce timestore i.e., maintain the same sequence of jobs, then o max would yield some bad sequence. But it is not guaranteed if o j can reproduce that sequence, or any sequence with some job missing its deadline. Intuitively, if there are two distinct values of offsets (bounded by its period) for a task, such that both yield the same sequence of jobs leading to the same job missing its deadline, any intermediate offset would result in the same behaviour, due to monotonocity. We can similarly minimize o i to obtain o min , and thus the offset interval [o min , o max ] for each task i.

div.head: C. Refining the offset space by constructing hyperboxes
div.p: We need to maximize (and minimize) each task offset individually, to preserve the soundness. The SMT solver Z3 thus needs to be invoked twice per task. Note that this cannot be posed as a multi-objective optimization problem to the Z3 solver as this results in unsound hyperboxes. As the sequence leading to a violation is already embedded (constrained) in the optimization problem, the time required for this step is expected to be much faster that the model checking step 1 .

These intervals can be composed to form a hyperbox in the offset space and are obvious candidates for rejection. The offset hyperbox composition is simply the cross-product of intervals obtained over all task offsets, which we denote as o min , o max .

To see why the composition is sound i.e., all offset values within the hyperbox lead to a deadline miss, consider a point in the hyperbox arrived at by increasing the offset values of the seed point. Observe that increasing task offsets corresponding to jobs scheduled during the waiting time of job j that missed its deadline, only worsens the start time of j, thus continuing the deadline miss.
Intuitively, if all offset values were to be uniformly increased (or decreased), the net effect is a "time-shift" of the sequence, preserving the deadline miss.

Similarly, consider another point in the hyperbox arrived at by decreasing the seed offsets. Decreasing offset values tends to create idle intervals during the waiting time of j, that could be allocated to j to meet its deadline. Recall that individual minimization of offsets still guarantees the deadline miss for j. Decreasing multiple offsets shifts the jobs in the "same" space, restricting the cumulative idle interval generated by offset reduction. This interval is no larger than the largest interval computed earlier by minimizing the offsets, thus preserving the deadline miss. We can similarly establish for mixed increasedecrease of values for offsets, thus generalizing over the entire hyperbox.

div.head: D. Iterative search algorithm
div.p: For each counterexample, we would like to obtain the largest possible hyperbox, corresponding to maximum size intervals of offsets and maximum number of tasks contributing to such intervals. This would allow us to quickly prune the space of offsets unsuitable for schedulability.

We assume that either the user provides bounds on the offset space, or the space is implicitly bounded by the periods of the respective tasks. Each iteration of the search procedure, presented in Algorithm 1, invokes Z3, each time refining the offset search space by rejecting these hyperboxes. The search terminates when (i) the model checker reports the property to be safe i.e., there is no job missing its deadline, in which case, any point in the remaining offset space can be chosen and the task set will be schedulable, or (ii) the hyperboxes cover the entire offset space, indicating the task set is unschedulable for any choice of offsets.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: We encoded the constraints representing the task sets and non-preemptive EDF and RM scheduling policies as a C program. The program takes as input the task specification consisting of task id, offset, jitter, period, BCET, WCET, Algorithm 1 Refining task offsets to yield schedulability T : task set under analysis ce: counterexample containing deadline miss j: job that missed its deadline in ce offsetspace: space of offset values reject = {}: the set of offset hyperboxes to be rejected while true do // construct constraints We then invoked CBMC with Z3 as its back-end solver to check if these task sets are schedulable. If a task set is not schedulable, Z3 produces a sequence of jobs (conforming to the task set specification) such that some job misses its deadline. A sample trace looks like:
div.formula: C 1 = Sched(T ) C 2 = ce timestore C 3 = e j > deadline j C 4 = offsetspace \ reject call Z3 to maximize offsets over C 1 ∧ C 2 ∧ C 3 ∧ C 4 call Z3 to minimize offsets over C 1 ∧ C 2 ∧ C 3 ∧ C 4 reject = reject ∪ o min , o max if reject ⊇
div.p: [tid,jid,cutoff,rel,start,end,deadline] [1,0,0,0,0,1,5] [0,0,3,3,3,9,13] ... [1,3,14,15,20,22,20] VERIFICATION FAILED // Task id 1, Job id 3, missed deadline From this, we generate a new C program with the constraints specified in Algorithm 1. This program is fed to Z3 (via CBMC) for maximization and minimization of offets subject to the encoded bounds.

To evaluate our approach, we randomly generated task sets containing 3 to 9 tasks. The periods were drawn randomly from a pre-defined set of values, so that the hyper period (least common multiple) is not too large, making the analysis tractable. In several cases, an offset point chosen outside the first discovered hyperbox (first refinement cycle), made the task set schedulable. For the unschedulable task sets, fewer than 6 hyperboxes (6 refinement cycles) were required to exhaust the entire offset space of the task sets.

In Tables II, III, and IV, we present experimental data for a small representative subset of the task sets, as listing all the generated task sets would occupy several pages. The columns #T and #R denote the number of tasks in the task set and the number of refinements carried out, respectively. Table II shows examples of task sets that are proven to be schedulable without any refinement. Table III shows examples of task sets that needed to be refined at most twice. Table IV shows examples of task sets were proven to be unschedulable after refinement. All experiments were conducted on a laptop with 8GB RAM, Intel i7 2.3GHz processor with Ubuntu 16.04 OS. For all experiments, the model checking and optimization analysis (refinement procedure) time was under 2 minutes.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: The use of model checking with our encoding allowed us to check schedulability, and where required, debug and refine offset values in practically acceptable time. In future, we would like to encode preemptive scheduling policies, support refining of period and WCET parameters of tasks and support scheduling on multicore processors. We would also like to investigate refining of parameters for message scheduling on communication protocols such as FlexRay and CAN.

figure.figDesc: The schedulability and other timing properties are encoded as assertions in the program. We use the CBMC model checker to analyze the assertions. The choice of a high-level language like C allows us to quickly encode the constraints and extend the model to more complex scheduling policies whenever required. Using CBMC as the model checker allows us to analyze the model with different backend solvers, including SAT (MiniSAT, Glucose) and SMT (Z3, Yices).
